utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case in open session, because yesterday we adjourned in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the appearances for the Prosecution, who is in the last row today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Stefan Waespi and Daryl Mundis, assisted by our case manager, Mr. Andres Vatter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis. And for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; and Alexis Demirdjian, legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On this day, the 15th of March, 2005, I bid good morning to all those present: The Prosecution, the Defence counsel, Mr. Bourgon, who is not here but I know he will join us tomorrow, and I also bid good morning to the accused and everybody in this courtroom or outside it who are assisting us in our work. Yesterday we addressed the question of planning. This is a matter that we will be addressing again tomorrow in the presence of Mr. Bourgon, but nevertheless I wish to draw attention to a small problem. It was suggested yesterday that we hear a witness on the 22nd of March in the morning. There are two problems there: The planning shows us that the courtrooms are occupied in the morning and that we cannot have a hearing on the 22nd of March in the morning. Either we move this witness to the 23rd of March in the morning, on condition that there is a courtroom, but the registrar tells me that there is no courtroom, or the other solution would be for this witness to testify on the 22nd of March in the afternoon and that the witness who starts on the 21st of March would not appear on the 22nd but would resume the following days. That is the small problem. Possibly this witness can only be available on the 22nd of March. If that is the case, then he has to be heard in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in view of the fact that the witness is available only on that day, we will hear that witness and then resume with the expert witness. But we would like to appeal to the Trial Chamber for the hearings of the expert witness to possibly take place both in the morning and in the afternoon so as to make up for the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, your idea is excellent, but as you know, we have three courtrooms and they are constantly occupied due to other cases. Occasionally there's a case that is postponed because the witness doesn't come and then this is a possibility. But I can't tell you in advance. As for the expert witness, you will do what you wish, but the expert witness has prepared a report, which is quite extensive. So we must focus only on some points in the report. This applies to the cross-examination as well. So there's no necessity to spend so much time with the expert witness, as we have a report which will be tendered. But that is after all your problem. It's up to you. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. This -- this is one of the issues that I will be prepared to address Your Honours on in more detail tomorrow morning. I have had discussions with Mr. Bourgon concerning the testimony of the expert and the Hadzihasanovic Defence team has informed me that they need three days for direct examination, the Kubura team needs one day for direct examination. Of course, our position is since he's a joint witness, we're entitled to equal -- a period of time combined, which would entitle us, in our respectful views, to four days of cross-examination. That consumes the entire eight-day period for which the witness is scheduled to testify, leaving no time for re-examination, nor for any questions that Your Honours might have following the eight days of direct and cross-examination. Our position, as I have informed the Defence, is in light of the fact that the witness has a 148-page expert report plus 310 pages of annexes, including a PowerPoint presentation, that -- that there is, in our respectful view, no need for them to spend four days on direct examination of the witness. But, again, I'm prepared to address Your Honours in more detail on that point tomorrow morning, when Mr. Bourgon is here. But our view, again, to be quite clear, is that, number one, eight days should be a sufficient period of time in total for the expert witness, but our -- our view is perhaps four days of direct examination might be a bit too much in light of the fact that there's some 460 pages of material that this expert has produced and which has now been filed and is before Your Honours. But, again, we'll leave that for more detailed discussion when Mr. Bourgon is back. But clearly we have a potential timing problem. And as Your Honour points out, we -- we are simply at the mercy of the -- of the Registry and the limitations in terms of the number of courtrooms that we have available and the large number of cases that are currently being heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any event, the question will be addressed again tomorrow, but between you, you can discuss it. I have read the expert report with interest, and there are points that are quite obvious, so there's hardly any need to ask questions about it, since the expert report has been -- or will be admitted into evidence. Perhaps eight days is a little too much. But it is a Defence expert, so you are entitled to ask him any questions you consider useful, but I must say that useful questions are those that will be useful for the Judges. It's to enlighten them. It's not to give you any particular pleasure. It's to inform the Judges. And a written report already provides a lot of information. But, of course, it may be contested in certain aspects, but anyway, we'll -- we'll talk about that tomorrow. Having said that the military expert witness of the Prosecution -- I don't remember how many days he took, but I think the Defence should have an equal amount of time from the standpoint of the equality of arms. Mr. Mundis, can you remind me? You probably know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution expert, General Reinhardt, took a total of five days, and the Prosecution spent one 90-minute session on direct examination in light of the fact that he had filed an expert report that was less than 50 pages long, and we spent 90 minutes on our direct examination and then the Defence, I believe, took some three, three and a half days to cross-examine him. So that certainly would be -- would be one way that the -- that this issue can be approached. I mean, again, the witness has a total of 450-plus pages that have been produced and filed, and -- and of course timing and scheduling issues are -- are completely in the hands of the Trial Chamber. But our -- our view is that in light of the large number of materials he's produced, four days very well might be considered excessive because of that expert report and also because of the time limitations and the courtroom and other resource limitations that we do face.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As the Judges meet daily to discuss matters, we will discuss this point too amongst ourselves and we will listen to you tomorrow with close attention, and then we will let you know what our decision is. But both parties have spoken. Does the other Defence team wish to intervene with regard to the expert witness? Because we've just been told that you need one day for your examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. We had estimated one day at the maximum to make sure that we did give ourselves sufficient time. But in reviewing the situation and also in light of what Your Honours and Mr. Mundis have said today, we could scale down the -- the amount of time that we would use. It was suggested one day at the maximum, and having spoken to Mr. Ibrisimovic now, I -- I think that we could reduce it to about two hours, depending on what were the most important issues that -- that needed to be raised from the report. So we will re-look at the matter and see whether we could reduce our time to make sure that the expert witness did finish by the 1st of April. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let us now proceed with the hearing of the witness. Can I ask the usher to be kind enough to bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. Let me check that the equipment is working and tell me whether you can hear and understand me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you have been called as a Defence witness for General Hadzihasanovic. Before asking you to read the solemn declaration, I need to know your first and last name, the place and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Zaim Mujezinovic. I was born on the 17th of July, 1966 in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm employed in the Army of the Federation as an officer. My rank is that of major.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. So you are a major in the army. And you have been assigned to what place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am working in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992/1993, did you have a position or a function? If so, which? And where were you deployed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992, I was employed in a company called Haril [phoen], engaged in defence and protection. As of the 15th of April, 1992, I became a member first of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina and later of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in the ABiH, what unit were you a member of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was first in the military police detachment of the District Staff of Territorial Defence, and then from the 1st of December, 1992 in the Military Police Battalion of the 3rd Corps as unit commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Major, have you testified in an international/national court before about the events that took place in your country, or is this the first time for you to testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am testifying for the first time about the wartime period of 1992/1993 and the events that took place in my country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you please read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Major, before giving the floor to the lawyers for the Defence, I will give you some explanations regarding the proceedings, as I do for all witnesses, so as to make sure that we can proceed in a smooth manner and in a productive manner. You will have to answer questions which will be put to you by the lawyers of General Hadzihasanovic, whom you certainly met in preparation of this hearing. Normally -- we plan to hear your testimony over a period of two days, today and tomorrow. As I was saying, you will be answering neutral questions, and your answers will have to be sufficiently detailed for the Judges to understand the answers you are giving to questions put to you. Upon the completion of this stage of the proceedings, which may perhaps last all morning, the Prosecution, which is seated to your right, will also be asking you questions within what is known as the cross-examination. And the duration of the cross-examination will be the same as the amount of time used by the Defence. But you will notice that the form of the questions during the cross-examination differ slightly from the type of questions put to you to the Defence, as during the cross-examination the Prosecution is entitled to ask you very leading questions, which you can answer with a yes or no. At the end of this stage, the Defence counsel may take the floor again for additional questions, which have to be linked to the questions put by the Prosecution. The three Judges, who are seated in front of you, may according to the Rules ask you questions at any time; however, as this is an adversarial procedure, we prefer to allow the parties to put to you their questions and only if we find that we need further clarification of some of your answers or because we feel that there may be some gaps in the answers, that we will ask you questions ourselves. After our questions, we give the floor once again to the Prosecution and the Defence for them to have the last word and to be able to respond to your answers given to the Judges' questions. Those would be in general terms the proceedings over the next two days. I also wish to draw your attention to two important points, which Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I am sure the Defence has already told you about, but it is my duty to remind you: You have taken the solemn oath to tell the whole truth, which excludes all false testimony, because false testimony is an offence which may be punished by this Tribunal. The second important point - which is more of a technical nature and which we have never encountered so far - but a witness may refuse to answer a question if he feels that his answer may one day be used against him, and the witness may say, "I don't wish to answer that question." In such an extremely exceptional case, the Chamber may intervene and compel the witness to answer nevertheless, while at the same time granting the witness immunity from prosecution, which means that what he says cannot be used before this Tribunal against him. This provision has been included in our Rules in order to contribute to the establishment of the truth. You will have to answer all these questions. As you perhaps know, this is a purely oral proceeding, so we don't know anything about you except for a very brief summary about what you are going to say. Hence, the importance of what you are going to tell us. And you will see a screen in front of you -- actually, you have two screens -- with words appearing in English, and you -- what you say will also be translated in English. And it is this that will be the transcript and the record of the proceedings; hence the importance of your answers. Therefore, if you don't understand the meaning of a question, ask the person putting it to you to rephrase it. We have plenty of time, and you can ask for a question to be rephrased. Should you have any difficulties, please don't hesitate to let us know, because we are here, among other things, to deal with any difficulties that might arise. For technical reasons and to give you a chance to have a rest, we are obliged to have a small break every hour and a half lasting 20 to 25 minutes, which will begin shortly. So from now until a quarter to 2.00, when we adjourn, we will be having two breaks, and the same applies to the hearing tomorrow. During these breaks, you will be able to take a rest because questions can be quite tiring, as you will see, and also the technicians have a chance to change the audiotapes. These breaks, let me assure you, are not intended for -- to give the Judges a rest. Having said that, I will give the floor to the Defence, who will add another piece of advice, and then they will embark upon their questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Examined by Ms. Residovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Mujezinovic.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As the Presiding Judge has just told you, I have a piece of advice, and I should like to ask you: In view of the fact that we both speak the same language, you can answer my questions straight away; however, both my question and your answers need to be interpreted so that Their Honours and our colleagues in the courtroom are able to follow. That is why I appeal to you that when you hear my question, you wait a few minutes before answering it, and I will do the same. Have you understood me?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that on the 1st of December, 1992 you became commander of the Military Police Battalion of the 3rd Corps. My question is: What duty did you perform throughout 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: During 1993, I was commander of the Military Police Battalion of the 3rd Corps of the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, who was your immediate superior? Your superior and the superior to the whole battalion.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The immediate professional superior was the security sector of the 3rd Corps, or the chief of the security sector of the 3rd Corps. According to the chain of command, the immediate superior was the commander of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The purview and tasks of the military police, were they regulated by any laws and regulations? And if so, tell us which.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: On the 8th of September, 1992, the Rules of Service for the military police was issued, which was the guideline for the work of both the Military Police Battalion and all other military police units. Also, the Law on Criminal Procedure and orders and instructions issued by the 3rd Corps were the main regulatory factors for the work of the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, could you briefly tell the Trial Chamber what were the main tasks of the military police and specifically the Military Police Battalion of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: As I have said, the Rules of Service defined the main principles and premises. The work of the military police consisted of implementing the powers of the military police and the services of the military police. When I say "the powers," there are 14 powers that every military policeman is allowed to resort to, from ID, identification, to filing of criminal reports. And when we are talking about military police services, there are seven elements that the military police has to observe. And these consist of the security service, meaning securing command posts, providing security for senior military officials and similar levels of command; then continuous duty service, which in practice means receiving and distributing information round the clock; the patrol service, which means control of the territory and ensuring respect of military discipline; the search service, and the name itself tells us it means searching on various grounds; the crime-prevention service, with the aim of preventing crime and also investigating crime; and the service for the regulation and control of military traffic, which means regulating traffic and movement of military convoys, individuals providing security in traffic for high-level military delegations, and the like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, who did you have authority over?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The military police unit primarily had authority over men in uniform; that is to say, members of the ABiH. This involved taking all steps in accordance with the law if a member of the ABiH had violated the law and the norms of military conduct. The military police also had competence with regard to civilians only if crimes were committed that involved the responsibility of the district military court. It was only in such cases that they had responsibility competence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, could you tell me which crimes are in question and are they regulated in instructions of any kind? I'm referring to crimes for which the military police could take action with regard to civilians too.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: This is regulated on the basis of the competence of military courts, and it involves acts that pose a danger to the vital interests of the army; that is to say, to the ABiH. These acts include subversive activity, sabotage activities, in order to weaken the force of the other side -- to weaken one's force. It also involved other acts of sabotage that posed a danger to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us who had responsibility over civilians, that is to say, individuals who were not members of the army, when other crimes were committed, not the crimes that are listed in the Law on Military Courts, as you have said?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: If civilians committed a crime of any kind or a misdemeanour of any kind which had nothing to do with the Law on Military Courts, then the Ministry of the Interior would be responsible for such crimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, how was your battalion -- how was your Military Police Battalion organised?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The Military Police Battalion was established and started functioning on the basis of temporary wartime establishment, which was then issued by the Main Staff of the ABiH, and it was the 3rd Corps' duty to implement these measures. In terms of the organisation, the battalion was composed of the following entities - and this depended on the situation - there was the command of the battalion of the military police, with the commander at its head -- or rather, his deputy. Within the command of the Military Police Battalion, there were various sectors which were responsible for the total organisation and functioning of the battalion. That means that the commander had his assistant for personnel affairs and later an assistant for security, an assistant for operations and training, and an assistant for logistics. And there were other factors, other officials in the command. There was a communications officer and other organisational levels. Together with the command battalion, the following entities were active: First, there was the detachment, and then the platoon for the services of the military police. They consisted of authorised officials -- or rather, of individuals who had been trained to conduct certain investigations. The composition depended on the situation, and apart from the authorised officials, there were soldiers who would be present, on duty, and to intervene; there were lawyers, et cetera. The following sector was composed of military police companies: Within those companies, according to the Rules of -- for the Military Police, there were certain main activities that they were involved in. The first company of the military police as a rule went on patrol. It was a traditional military police unit. The second one was to provide security at various levels. The third one usually engaged in direct combat in the field. And the fourth one was a traffic unit, and it focussed on regulating military traffic. Subsequently, on the basis of demonstrated need, I think it was in the second half of 1993, a company for anti-terrorist activity was formed, which was in fact first a platoon and was then transformed into a company. Its main objective was to engage in combat against anti-sabotage units, to deal with complex situations, to go on patrol, provide security for high-ranking military officials, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, tell me, since you were the military police commander in the 3rd Corps from the time it was established, what was the strength of the battalion, of the Military Police Battalion, when it was established and did this change in the course of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The core of the Military Police Battalion was composed of a company of military police from the District Territorial Defence Staff. From the 1st of December until the end of the war, this corps was transformed and the battalion was formed in accordance with temporary establishment, as I have already said. The men didn't have adequate training - that's quite sure - for the simple reason that we didn't have sufficient databases in order to mobilise into the military police unit men who fulfilled the conditions, men who were on record as being fit for such service. Secondly, the battalion was formed at the same time that certain tasks were being carried out, so that it wasn't in a position to establish a structure such as it would have established in peacetime conditions. Thirdly, the ABiH - and that means the battalion too - was formed out of nothing. So the equipment that the Military Police Battalion had depended exclusively on the goodwill that existed on the possibility of mobilising such equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You haven't told me how many members the Military Police Battalion had.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I think in the first half of 1993 the Military Police Battalion had between 200 and 250 men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that it was transformed as tasks were being carried out. Could you assess the number of members in the battalion towards the end of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it would be logical for the battalion in 1993 to have about 400 to 450 men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A minute ago you mentioned the composition and structure of the battalion in terms of companies. How many members of the battalion of the military police would enter the composition of certain companies?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: As a rule, the military police companies were in organisational terms similar to infantry companies. They were formed of the command of the company and three platoons. Each platoon had three detachments in total. This means that one detachment would have about eight men and a platoon would have 25 men - 24 men plus the commander, who would be the 25th - so the companies had between 75 and 80 men, in terms of establishment. The strength depended on a number of factors: On the legal situation, on authorisation from the superior command, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that within the battalion there was a service that was involved in police investigations and military investigations -- military police investigations. How many men were there in that service? Since you said that at the beginning it was the size of a detachment and later of a platoon. Could you be more precise and tell me how many members of the Military Police Battalion were engaged in that service.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I think there were a little more than 20 men because as a rule one would work around the clock. When I said "a permanent service," it was in the platoon for investigations, and this meant that it was always your obligation to have a certain number of men by the phone who could answer the phone and you needed a certain number of soldiers and officers who could intervene, depending on the situation. There were about six soldiers who were engaged, and depending on the situation, two or four lawyers were engaged; again, depending on the situation, a certain number of authorised officials were engaged, officials who were involved in operations. Alone there were about four to six of them. Again, that depended on the situation. Later there were perhaps more of them. And if necessary, a certain number of professional soldiers would be added -- a certain number of mobilised soldiers would be added to carry out certain activities in the field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to these regular tasks that you carry out and that related to the services of the military police, tell me, in which situations and when did the military police react to information on crimes having been perpetrated?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: When it came to light that the crime had been perpetrated, the military police would go to the scene of the crime. If there were indications according to which the crime had been committed by a member of the ABiH, the first obligation, apart from going to the scene, was to inform the duty investigative judge. Upon arriving on the scene, the military police would seal off the area where a crime had been committed, wait for the investigative judge to arrive, and take further action in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. accordance with the instructions that the investigative judge had issued. That means that the investigative judge at that point in time took charge of all future actions, all future steps, taking -- collecting certain evidence, et cetera. If the judge did not go to the scene -- or rather, if this was not necessary, the military police would then take the necessary steps at the scene in order to detect the perpetrator. Then an operations plan would be compiled in order to find the perpetrator of the crime, to put everything on paper and to file a criminal report, which would be forwarded to the competent court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, tell me whether in this pre-trial phase, did the military police always act independently when they found out about a crime having been committed or were there any situations in which they would act together with the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: This depended on the indications -- or rather, on the elements that pointed to the perpetrator of the crime. If there were elements of crime that pointed to a civilian as a perpetrator of the crime, then, as a rule, action would be taken with the Centre for Security -- or rather, the Ministry of the Interior. Then we would compile a joint plan, and when the military police was no longer responsible, the civilian would take over -- the civilian police would take over to find the perpetrator of the crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A minute ago you mentioned the fact that you would inform the duty -- or rather, the investigative judge that you suspected that a crime had been committed, and when the judge went to the scene of the crime, the judge in fact took charge of all the measures that would then be taken. When the investigative -- or rather, duty judge went to the scene of the crime, did members -- could members of the military police act independently and contrary to the instructions issued by the judge, regardless of the fact that you perhaps might order the soldier to act in a contrary manner?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: No. The military police did not have the authority to act in such a manner, nor did anyone else have the authority to act in such a manner. It wasn't possible to act contrary to the instructions of the duty -- or rather, investigative judge who went to the scene of the crime. According to the law, when the judge arrives at the scene of the crime, he takes charge of all the activities that are to be taken in order to find the perpetrator of the crime -- or rather, in order to punish the perpetrator of a crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, when the investigative judge went to the scene of the crime or when you in other situations gathered information on the perpetrator of a crime, when you gathered sufficient information on the basis of which you could institute criminal proceedings, who would you forward this evidence -- or, rather, information to?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: It was our duty to forward that evidence -- or, rather, all the other elements that might be gathered and that might be sufficient to institute criminal proceedings, to the prosecutor, to the competent prosecutor. We proceeded in two ways: A criminal report would be filed with the relevant information and with an assessment -- a proposal for an assessment of the crime; and secondly, the prosecutor's office might be provided with the report alone, without a description of the factual situation, only with the elements that pointed to the perpetrator of a crime, and then the prosecutor could later assess the crime and forward the matter to the judge in charge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, according to the law, was it your duty to provide a factual description of a crime and to provide a legal description of the crime? And if that is what you did, as you just said, would your assessment, your legal assessment, your description of the crime in any way bind the prosecutor to whom you would forward this material?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: According to the law, it was not our duty to provide a factual description of the crime or to propose an assessment of the crime. In accordance with established practice and the fact that military courts had a lot of duties, we compiled criminal reports in accordance with their instructions and we provided a factual description and proposed legal assessment of the crime, simply in order to assist in preparing for the case and shedding light on the case. So it wasn't our duty to provide a factual description or to propose an assessment -- a legal assessment of the crime, because the responsibility for the assessment of a crime was the prosecutor's, and it was the judge to finally take a decision on how a crime should be described.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. To date a number of individuals have testified before this Chamber, and they have spoken about the chain of command in the military police. This is why I will only briefly ask you who was in charge of the military police, who was in command of the military police, and how did this individual command the military police?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: According to the Rules for the Military Police and in accordance with practice in the field, the way in which the military police would be commanded was defined. According to one of the items, the commander of the unit within which the military police is established commands the military police, and the command is formed of the security service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, tell me whether in 1993 these rules on commanding were not respected. And if so, in what way and how long did this situation last?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact time, but for a brief period the practice that was followed was bad, so to speak. The Chief of Staff tried to take over actions taken by the corps commander, not because he was capricious but because all the other units, such as Military Police Battalions, were almost under the Chief of Staff. As an example, I'm referring to the Engineers Battalion and to other units of that kind. And on that basis, the Chief of Staff for a certain period of time, a brief period of time, tried to have command over the Military Police Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, a minute ago you said that the commander through his professional organ governed -- commanded the military police. Tell me, what sort of authority did the security organ have when it comes to commanding, in professional terms, the Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in professional terms, everything of a military police nature is the responsibility of the security sector -- or rather, of its chief in the 3rd Corps. In professional terms, commanding the military police involves coordinating, issuing orders, instructions, and other elements that can contribute to correctly resolving certain military police situations. This means contact between the Military Police Battalion and the security sector was not -- I wouldn't say "daily," but it took place every hour in order to ensure that everything was legal and that military police methods were properly implemented. The chief of security in fact had all information on the work of the Military Police Battalion. He issued additional orders or provided further guidelines for action. With regard to all these actions, he had to provide the 3rd Corps command -- commander with information and obtain further instructions on action to be taken from him. The 3rd Corps commander had exclusive authority to issue orders to engage the Military Police Battalion in combat -- or rather, it was his exclusive authority to issue orders for the Military Police Battalion to be engaged, apart from cases in which assistance had to be provided in certain areas and certain tasks had to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Mujezinovic, whether in the area of the 3rd Corps in subordinate units, were there also military police units or was the Military Police Battalion the only police force, to put it that way, of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The Military Police Battalion was not the sole military police force of the 3rd Corps. Within each of the brigades, depending on its structure or purpose, there was a platoon or company of military police. Within operative groups, depending on the actual needs on the ground, a military police company would be active. In this way, it was possible for the military police to do its work where it is actually deployed within the BH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, these platoons or military police companies in the brigades and operative groups, did they have all the original powers and competencies as the Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Rules of Service for the military police, the Law on Criminal Procedure, orders and instructions of the 3rd Corps in effect provided the guidelines for the work of all military police units within the 3rd Corps. The competencies and services are universal in nature, and the fact that there is military police means that these rules have to be applied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Mujezinovic, who was in command and control of the platoons and companies of the military police in subordinate units and how was this control and command exercised?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The platoons or companies of military police in brigades and operative groups were also structured according to provisional wartime establishment, and the platoons and companies were headed by a military police commander. His professional superior body was the assistant commander for security in the relevant brigade or operations group. And the responsible person for combat engagement of military police units at that level was the brigade commander, the commander of the brigade within whose structure was the military police unit or, if it was an operations group, the commander of the operations group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Military Police Battalion of the 3rd Corps and you as the commander, did you have any authority to control and command companies and platoons in subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: According to the hierarchy and according to the regulations, the Military Police Battalion did not have any superior -- superiority over military police companies and platoons within operations groups or brigades. Our relationship was based exclusively on 3rd Corps orders and possibly there may be coordination on the ground to deal with certain crisis situations, to find perpetrators of criminal offences, and the like. But the Military Police Battalion did not have any authority to issue orders towards companies or platoons of the military police in the brigades.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the customary tasks that you had in relation to companies and platoons? Did you have any duties or obligations that were not of a command nature?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: We were not entitled to any reprisals or measures without orders from the corps command. What would usually happen was that a military police platoon or company in the field was not physically or for -- in terms of personnel and equipment, able to deal with a certain situation and to take military police measures. In that case, the corps commander most frequently, upon the proposal of the chief of security of the 3rd Corps, would issue the order to engage parts of the Military Police Battalion, to assist or carry out certain tasks in the field together with the platoon or company of military police. The brigade military police and operations group military police with relation to the battalion, had only one obligation, and that was to forward daily or weekly reports about their activities exclusively of a numerical nature, and the Military Police Battalion would pool those factors and pass them -- forward them on to the security sector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please explain: What do you mean a report of a numerical nature? A military police platoon or company needs to report to you about what exactly?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The General Staff of the BH army prepared a form -- a format for reports on measures taken and activities of military police units in accordance with their competencies and services, and these forms were passed on to the 3rd Corps and then the 3rd Corps organised a system of reporting. This report consisted exclusively of numerical indicators of measures taken. By way of example, the form was as follows: Military police of the X brigade has undertaken the following measures. For example, cautioned 18 soldiers; identified 6; escorted 4 persons, et cetera. And on the basis of these numerical data, a composite report would be compiled, and then the Military Police Battalion would forward these reports to the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, if in an area in which a platoon or company of the military police was active a crime were to be committed, my first question is: Who would be entitled to act in accordance with the powers of the military police? Would it be the military police of that unit, and did they have to report to you or to someone else about this, and what were the competencies or possibilities for the battalion's engagement in accordance with the rules and the practice in the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The competence with respect to all investigative work in order to discover the perpetrator of a criminal offence was within the hands of the military police unit which had territorial jurisdiction. By way of example, if a criminal offence is committed in the 318th Brigade, the scene would be secured by the military police for the 318th Brigade. Their duty service would inform the military judge on duty and then would act in accordance with his instructions. If there are no elements for the competent -- territorially competent judge to go on site, then the military police makes its own assessment and prepares a plan for discovering the perpetrator of the crime. It informs the assistant commander for security - in this case of the 318th Brigade - of all measures taken. And in accordance with his competencies and powers, he would then coordinate those activities on the ground and would at the same time inform the chief of the security sector of the 3rd Corps about all measures and steps taken to discover the perpetrator of the crime or the measures and acts that he plans to do in the forthcoming period. On the basis of those reports, the chief of security makes a judgement as to whether that territorially competent unit of the military police is competent or not competent, but whether they are capable of implementing all these measures. And if so, he lets them finish the work; if not, he makes a proposal to the corps commander that he orders the use of parts of the Military Police Battalion to help in elucidating the crime. So the military police is not obliged to provide detailed reports to the Military Police Battalion but only to simply list the measures taken in numerical form. A complete report goes along this other line of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. command, and on the basis of that final assessment is the Military Police Battalion engaged or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Mujezinovic, were parts of the Military Police Battalion engaged in, conditionally speaking, within the territorial competence of platoons or companies of individual brigades?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Military Police Battalion was frequently - I don't know exactly how frequently - pursuant to orders of the 3rd Corps commanders engaged to implement certain military police measures in certain areas outside its own framework of activity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If a part of the Military Police Battalion is engaged in a particular area upon orders of the commander, tell me, would you be in command of those parts of the battalion or does the chain of command change in that case?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The corps commander's order in principle contains instructions as to command. If we go back to the story about the work of military police units and the assistant for security, you will see that the chief of security is the most competent individual to propose an engagement of units of the Military Police Battalion and on the basis of that proposal, the 3rd Corps commander renders the decision. Now, the part of the Military Police Battalion is resubordinated to the unit to whose territory that part is being deployed or that part of the battalion may act independently, depending on the elements of the order, that is, whether it is resubordination or independent activity. This determines the principle of reporting to the commanding officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as I would like to use certain documents with this witness, I would like to ask the bundle of documents that we have prepared for the Trial Chamber and the witness to be handed out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, will you please look at document number 51.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is document DH161, doc 4, and it is an order of the command of the 3rd Corps dated the 24th of April, 1993. Are you familiar with this document? And if you are, tell me, does it reflect one of those situations when the Military Police Battalion was engaged in the way you have just described?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I am familiar with the document, and it fully reflects what I just said. If you read it carefully, you will see that the unit is being resubordinated to the commander of the 325th Brigade. And in military language, he is responsible for the continued engagement and use of the military police unit. Also, the 3rd Corps commander is authorising the commander of the 325th Brigade to assess himself when the obligations of the Military Police Battalion cease, when it can go back to its normal position. In military terms, everything is clear in this order, with respect to the engagement, responsibilities, right to issue orders, and reporting with respect to the military police unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, in connection with this order, whether the preamble to the order indicates the reasons why the commander has decided to resubordinate a part of the battalion to this brigade, which you referred to earlier on.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the preamble the reasons are given for this order issued by the 3rd Corps commander. The content of this introduction is based on a report received, because it says that "because of the factual situation on the ground."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you look at document at tab 47. This is the order of the 3rd Corps commander dated the 16th of June, 1993, DH161, document 13. Tell me, do you know whether a part of your battalion was engaged to provide security in the area of Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with this order, too. And a part of the unit that I was in command of was engaged in this area. Once again, the same principle applies, that the corps commander issued an order on the basis of an assessment of the situation and with a view to preventing undesirable activities. The commander has decided together with military police units of the brigade who were deployed in the area to engage a part of the Military Police Battalion. It is the duty of the commander of the 306th Brigade as a result of this order for all the military police elements of the 306th, the 312th, and a part of the Military Police Battalion to place them under his command and to take the necessary measures with these units to carry out the order of the 3rd Corps commander. So he is responsible for the implementation of measures and for reporting to the 3rd Corps command on the measures taken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us go back once again to the part of your testimony that referred to the actual establishment of the battalion and the efforts made to improve it. Tell me, after the decision was made to set up a Military Police Battalion, the nucleus of which was the Military Police Company of the District Staff, to what extent did the 3rd Corps commandant commander devote attention to the training of the battalion and what efforts were necessary in view of the problems that were encountered?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: In answer to the first part of your question, the 3rd Corps command and its commander did devote special attention and significance to the formation and structuring of military police units, that is, the battalion of the military police, primarily in order to form a unit that would be -- that would set an example to other units of the 3rd Corps but also to improve the military discipline in all other parts of the 3rd Corps. The Military Police Battalion encountered a series of problems in the course of its development and maturing. First of all, in terms of personnel, because, as I said before, it was difficult to find the right people. I wish in particular to underline that we never had any constraints or limitations from the 3rd Corps in terms of the ethnic selection of personnel. The only guiding principle was the capability of people and their ability to carry out assigned tasks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Mujezinovic, since you were in a company of the District Staff, what duty were you performing?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: First I was platoon commander. And when Mr. Husic, the commander, left the District Staff, I was appointed commander of the Military Police Company of the District Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as company commander, which later became the nucleus of the Military Police Battalion of the 3rd Corps of the ABiH, were you aware of the efforts of the 3rd Corps commander to form a unified battalion of the armed forces of both the HVO and the army as a precondition for the discipline of forces in the area? Or perhaps you were not aware of that at the time.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, I was not aware of that for the simple reason that the corps commander made his decision to form the battalion on the 1st of December, 1992, and that is when I learnt that I would be the battalion commander. The efforts made by the corps command I became aware of later for the simple reason that I personally encountered problems, especially with respect to my subordinates who were not of Bosniak ethnicity. And the 3rd Corps command told me that from the beginning the HVO was offered the possibility to be a component part of the Military Police Battalion on an equal footing in the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the break, I should like to ask you to look at the document at tab 1. It is a document of the 3rd Corps command dated the 27th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is a new document, though we spoke about it with another witness, but it was not produced. We have given a copy to the Prosecution, and there is an English translation. So I ask for permission to use this document in the examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, is this a document that confirms what you learnt subsequently, and that is that the 3rd Corps commander from the very beginning wished to unite the military police of the armed forces that were in the area?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this document confirms this. And I wish to underline in particular that from this document and subsequent correspondence within the 3rd Corps the general position of the corps command and probably the commander was evident, and that is for the ABiH to reflect the ethnic composition of the population. I think this can be seen from these documents. We used the Croatian language, and I, too, for a moment -- for a period of time was referred to as the "zapovjednik," and not "komandant," which is the Croatian term, so this also reflected these efforts. We used both languages equally.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps now would be the best moment for the break. And I would like the witness to be given this set of documents so he could have better insight into them, and that would ensure our smooth work after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the break, Major, cast a glance at the documents that have been given to you, which will facilitate the work of the Defence after the break. It is 10.30, we will resume at about five to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now resume. The Defence may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, before the break, you mentioned certain problems that you yourself found out about when attempting to mobilise into the ABiH on an equal basis members of the Croatian population; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, to that effect, did you react -- or rather, did your men have problems because they were in the army and did you react to that situation?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Members of the Military Police Battalion who were of Croatian nationality had certain problems when working and living outside the unit. There was psychological pressure and direct pressure from so-called good Croats and other individuals who were HVO members, and I think that I wrote something about this. At the very beginning of the establishment of the battalion the purpose of this report was to inform my superior command but also to obtain instructions and to tell the corps command that action should be taken in relation to other social and political organs in order to prevent the abuse, the mistreatment of Croats in the Military Police Battalion and in other ABiH units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have a look at document under tab 5, DH2077, and tell me, is this what you have testified? Is this the warning that you mentioned that you drafted when the battalion was being formed?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's an official record -- an official note of mine which I drafted and forwarded to the corps command, and it reflects the actual situation at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, in addition to the fact that orders were issued in order to discipline the army, did the corps command and your battalion take other measures apart from the order that was issued in order to implement such orders?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Issuing orders was the first stage. After the corps command had issued orders, usually a team from the corps command would go into the field. And as far as organisation -- military organisation, disciplinary measures are concerned, combat readiness, et cetera, they -- there would usually be officials from the 3rd Corps who would go upon orders from the commander in order to ensure that there was such a situation. In order to assist in the field, remove shortcomings for me in the unit and for other commanders, this was an opportunity to mention the problems we had as far as organisation was concerned and to inform the corps command about how they could assist me in order to resolve any difficulties that I'd encountered. With regard to the measures I had to take and with regard to disciplining the troops, it was necessary to have feedback information. If I received an order from the corps command in order to take certain police measures in the field, it was my duty at the same time to inform them of the action taken -- or rather, to propose other activities, measures, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Mujezinovic, during the break you probably had the opportunity of having a look at this series of documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would now like to show the witness document 6, 9, 17 and 19. These are new documents and we only have these documents in the B/C/S language. I'd like to show the witness these documents in order to identify them; whereas, as far as the other documents that the witness has had a look at are concerned, I only have a few questions -- a few general questions about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Proceed as usual. Ask the witness to read the relevant paragraphs so that the Prosecution can refer to these documents in the course of its cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, could you please have a look at document under number 6. A minute ago, you mentioned steps that were necessary to take in order to ensure that the security organ and the military police were well prepared. To identify the document itself and in order to put my question to you, could you please read out the person who issued the document, the number of the document, the subject, who is it addressed to, and on page 1 read out paragraph 1 and the last paragraph on page 1.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The document was drafted by the 3rd Corps security sector, and it mentions the chief of the security sector, Ramiz Dugalic. He signed the document. The subject is "Duties and tasks of the military security service of the ABiH armed forces." It's addressed to the commands of all brigades and to the Municipal Defence Staff -- I apologise, to the Municipal Defence Staffs, and to assistant commanders for security. Paragraph 1 is as follows: "Train officials to bring up to strength the military service security, to bring up -- to appoint people to establishment posts from officials to the security administration of the Main Staff -- the Supreme Command Staff."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the last item? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: "Combat against crime in units, protection of weapons, ordnance and military equipment is also the permanent task of the military security service."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In order to identify the document, could you just have a look at document under tab 9. It's a document from the 3rd Corps command dated the 1st of April. I apologise -- yes, it's a document from the 3rd Corps dated the 7th of April, 1993. Could you tell us the number of the document and what the document is about.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The number of the document is 04/1008-3. The subject is a warning. It was signed by the Chief of Staff, Mr. Muradif Mekic. The document is about a warning issued to certain units for failing to implement a previous order which had to do with forwarding a proposal to appoint a judge for the military misdemeanours court, the military disciplinary court that was to be established within the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please have a look at document number 17 so that we can identify it. It's a document from the security sector dated the 31st of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The same is true -- or also he should have been asked, I think in relation to all these documents, whether he has seen it, he has received it, and -- and things like that, sort of a foundation. But having said that, I believe it goes at the end of the day to -- to the weight a document is given. I don't object, you know, to these documents. They appear on the record to be -- to be okay, but I just wanted to state that for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: (redacted), you must have good reason to do so. But Prosecution would like to know what this good reason is. Is that correct? That's what you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. And if we could briefly go into private session for a moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are back in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The document that you have just described in this way, dated the 31st of August, 1993, tell me, was it simple and easy to satisfy the criteria demanded by your professional organ in order to bring up to strength the military police and the military security organ, and was it possible for these criteria to be met -- to be fully met in 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, to be quite objective, it was very difficult to respect these principles when it comes to checking up and engaging certain soldiers and officers into military police units. First of all, a unified data -- a unified database, because there were a lot of displaced persons, was not functioning in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina -- didn't exist in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. As an example, you quite often were not able to check up on certain individuals unless there was a statement from an official from the military police. You didn't have any other documents which would enable you to check how well-trained or how well-prepared a given individual was. That's the first thing. And secondly, even if you had all this information, it was difficult in the territory under the 3rd -- under the control of the 3rd Corps to find a sufficient number of people who were sufficiently well-trained in order to be military police officers -- or rather, soldiers in the military police units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us now look at document at tab 19, which is also only in B/C/S, and tell me, who is the author of the document? What does it relate to? And are you familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am fully familiar with the document. It is an order by the commander of the 3rd Corps, signed on behalf of the commander by someone, but which was sent to all the other units located in Zenica in addition to the battalion of the military police. Actually, by this order the corps commander is endeavouring by properly engaging military police units to prevent all forms of abuse of authority, to prevent any potential attempt to commit a criminal offence, and to discipline the soldiers within the units located in that area so as to ensure that they behaved properly as soldiers and looked like soldiers and implemented the norms, regulations, and orders applying to members of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, I wish to say it is document "Strictly confidential," 03/100-391-2, dated the 20th of October, 1993, and the corps commander has addressed them to commands of units located in Zenica, and this is a document I have already shown to Mahir Izet, but it is in B/C/S. We still have not received the English translation of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, as we have been speaking about ways of training and equipping the security sector and the military police service and during the break you were able to look through these documents, I would like to ask you to tell me whether the documents listed in this first chapter - and for the record, I will identify them: Document number 17, dated the 17th of January, 1992, request issued by the command of the 3rd Corps; document P324, at tab 2; the document at tab 3, 0542; document at tab 4, DH0708; document at tab 5, DH2077; document at tab 6, security sector document dated the 19th of March, 1993; at tab 7, document DH787; document at tab 8, DH805; document at tab 9, 04/1008-3, dated the 7th of April, 1993; document at tab 10, 0840; document at tab 11, DH156/1; document at tab 12, number 1002; document at tab 13, DH160/5; document at tab 14, DH160/6; document at tab 15, number 1364; document at tab 16, number 1408; document at tab 17, it is a document of the security sector, number 03/100-291-3 dated the 31st of August, 1993; document at tab 18, DH1552; and document at tab 19 of the 3rd Corps command, number 03/100-391-2 of the 20th of October, 1993. Tell me, Mr. Mujezinovic, having looked at all these documents, are these documents which indicate that efforts were made within the framework of the 3rd Corps command that you testified about beforehand?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I know that and appreciate the fact that the Defence want to speed up the -- the proceedings, but I think it's a highly leading way, the way it's done here. Documents which the witness may have seen during the break, but they are of so different nature, different authors. Some of them have not been translated into B/C/S, which is my problem, not the witness's. I'm not sure whether it's -- it's a helpful question now to sum it up in a leading way and -- and ask him whether that really reflects what he has said before, that appropriate measures were -- will be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you submit them one by one, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am in your hands, but I believe that with previous witnesses, with your permission, especially in the case of witnesses with a lot of documents, like Dzemal Merdan, I applied the same procedure. But there's no problem. I can ask the witness to briefly comment on each document. The documents that were not translated, with your permission I showed them to the witness, and he has commented on them. And now we can go through them one by one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Document at tab 2, P324, can you please just tell me what it is about, this document. What is the subject of this document? And are you aware of it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just an observation: I have no problem for these documents to come in as such, but it's, I think, just not helpful if he's led to comment on documents he has not seen before, as he has testified a couple of times. I don't think it makes any sense to go through document by document. The documents which he has seen, perhaps drafted, there he can comment. Otherwise, the documents speak for themselves. And Ms. -- the Defence can argue it in -- in its closing. That's just my Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. observation. It's in your hands how -- and, of course, in Ms. Residovic's hands, how she wants to -- to conduct the examination-in-chief of these 18 documents. We certainly have time, because it's the only witness remaining. But again, we don't have objections if the documents come in as such because they speak for themselves. But I have difficulties to have this witness comment on documents he has not authored, he has not seen before, especially in the leading form. The Defence has operated by asking: Does that confirm what you have -- what you have said before?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. By example, document 2, the Defence could ask the witness whether he's familiar with this document, which has to do with a meeting that was held on the 30th of December, 1992 at 9.00 in the morning. Maybe he attended the meeting, so he can say, "Yes, I am aware of it" or "I am not," and we can go through it quickly. So please ask the witness whether he knows this document; and if he doesn't, is he aware of the contents of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, document number 2, P324, is an announcement of a meeting of legal services. Tell me, do you know that such meetings were held, did you attend those meetings, and do you know anything about the subjects discussed at such meetings?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of orders of this kind and similar orders dealing with the legal activities within the 3rd Corps. In the initial stage, I would attend those meetings, but then later, depending on the subject matter, one of my associates, the lawyers from the Military Police Platoon would attend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, look at document number 3. It is Defence Exhibit 542. Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is a document of the Military Police Battalion command dated the 5th of January, 1993. Who is the signatory of this document and what does it represent in the process of development of the Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I certainly am the signatory of this document, and it speaks about the deployment of personnel and their appointment to various duties within the Military Police Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now please look at document number 4, numbered DH708, and which was issued by the command of the 3rd Corps on the 4th of February, 1993, and tell me, do you recognise this document which is entitled "The work of security organs of the military police"?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because the activities of the police units of which I was a commander are covered by this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As in paragraph 2, listing the localities among which Zenica figures, is this a document which specifies or perhaps confirms what you said as to who had the original competence in a particular area?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this document confirms the jurisdiction of certain units of the military police over particular areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of the fact that I already showed you documents 5 and 6, now please look at document number 7, DH787, and tell me, please, whether this, too, is a document you are familiar with and which refers to meetings of judicial organs that you commented on when speaking about document at tab 2.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the original document, but I do know that the lawyers from the military police did attend this meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look at document number 8, DH0805, and the document I showed you before, that is, document at tab 9, dated the 7th of April, 1993, and tell me whether you are aware that there was a military disciplinary court in the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please. We're talking about document 8; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, 9, I understand, before 8. And we don't have a translation for 9. If briefly the heading could be read out and some other features which allow us to familiarise ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness has already explained this document, but I would suggest that the witness look at documents at 8 and 9, as the document at 9 refers to document at 8, so the witness can answer both questions at the same time, both the one asked by me and by my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The document at 8 is "Instructions of the 3rd Corps to all units to submit a proposal of persons who would take part in forming the military disciplinary court." And the document at 9 is an additional request to units who did not carry out the provisions of the previous document. These are personnel proposals for the appointment of persons to the military disciplinary court in the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, please look at document 10, which is 0840, and tell me: Do you recognise this document, or did tasks for the Military Police Battalion emanate from this document?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the document is addressed to commands of all brigades, of staff units, and all Municipal Defence Staffs. Actually, the battalion is engaged on two grounds: First, in the area of military police activities; and secondly, within our own unit that we should detect potential perpetrators of criminal offences who may have committed theft, robbery, and the like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In connection with the two previous documents that you said referred to the election of judges to the court, did the Military Police Battalion have any competencies in reporting army members for disciplinary misdemeanours?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. With regard to disciplinary procedures against members of the army of the 3rd Corps, the police battalion did have certain responsibilities, and these had to do with the establishment of the facts and filing a request for conducting disciplinary proceedings to the unit to which the perpetrator belonged. That is where the competencies of the military police cease.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now look at document at 11, DH156/1. A moment ago you spoke about how the implementation of orders was monitored. Tell me, are you aware of this document, and is it a reflection of one way of monitoring the implementation of orders that you have already testified about?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I am familiar with this order. It is just one in a series of orders issued by the 3rd Corps with a view to establishing the actual state of affairs in the units, their organisation, and readiness to carry out set assignments. Orders of this kind are welcome for subordinate units, for me in particular, as from my superiors I would receive an assessment on the basis of their personal insight into the actual state of affairs, so I was able to seek assistance for any particular issue that could have been addressed at the level of the 3rd Corps command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now look at document at tab 12, please. It is only in B/C/S. It is document 1002. And as it is a document of the security sector, 03/100-113-4, tell me, what does this document refer to? You will read the second paragraph, please, and the fourth paragraph so that I can ask you a question about it.
