utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me which you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The document speaks about the increase of all forms of crime in units of the 3rd Corps of the ABiH army and then tasks. So please read out this paragraph: "By previous orders ..." You can read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: "By previous orders, guidelines, and assignments, members of the military security service and the military police were obliged to undertake all measures and acts within the framework of their competencies with a view to detecting and preventing all types of criminal activity."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Read now the one-but-last paragraph: "All members ..."

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: "All the members of the military security service and the military police who are not ready or are afraid to carry out their functional duties and obligations as prescribed by the Rules of Service for the military security service should immediately say so and leave the military security service and the military police and let those duties be taken over by those who are ready to meet all their obligations, even at the cost of their own lives, as we all swore to do when we joined the ranks of the RBiH army."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, are you familiar with this document of the security sector? And within the military police ranks, did you encounter the kind of problems referred to in this document -- or rather, did you take steps to implement these tasks within the 3rd Corps Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I am familiar with this document, and the command of the Military Police Battalion undertook a series of steps to carry out both this and all previous documents relating to this area of activity. Of course, because of the problems we had with the availability of personnel, there were certain problems that we encountered, because all members of the military police were not absolutely conscientious and disciplined and soldierlike, and in relation to such persons we took steps to discipline them. We would reassign them to another unit, or possibly pass even harsher punishment on them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, did any member of the Military Police Battalion -- was any member spared for any omissions or acts they may have committed?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: No, not a single member of the Military Police Battalion was spared. On the contrary, all of them who violated in any way the military discipline or the Code of Conduct of military policemen were punished more drastically than regular members of the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Mujezinovic, were members of the military police briefed on their obligation to respect the Geneva Conventions and other rules of warfare?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: In principle, all of them were familiarised on a number of occasions. If they came with some prior knowledge, then they knew that already, and then through training that we undertook within the unit a special course was in respect of Geneva Conventions and other customary war law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you look at document at tab 13, DH160, document 5, whereby the commander of the 3rd Corps is providing information about criminal acts against humanity and international law to all operative groups, independent brigades, and headquarters units. Were you one of those independent units?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the document and is this one of the ways in which you were informed about the obligation to respect war law?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I am familiar with the document, and this was just one of the ways in which the unit that I commanded was familiarised with crimes against humanity and international law. On the basis of this document, in the unit, in accordance with our training plans, we studied this area specifically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now look at document at tab 14, DH160/6. Earlier you spoke about materiel constraints in the battalion. Are you familiar with this document? And is it linked to what you have told us so far about efforts to improve training and to ensure the materiel preconditions for your military policework?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the original of this document, but the chief of the security sector did inform me about a document that had reached the 3rd Corps, and on the basis of that document and cooperation established with the Security Services Centre in Zenica, training started of members of the Military Police Battalion for the execution of certain crime technical activities within the framework of pre-trial investigations and procedures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, what was the policy of the 3rd Corps and its commander regarding respect of the law -- or rather, to what extent were you asked or requested to fully implement the rule of law.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The principle of law has to be respected without any exceptions. This was underlined at briefings with the corps commander. And when information was provided by the chief of the security service, they said that special attention should be paid to respecting the law and to implementing military norms and to disciplining all members of the army, and in particular members of the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever have direct communication -- direct contact with Commander Hadzihasanovic with regard to these issues, and were you familiar with his standpoint that he -- respect -- in relation to how the Military Police Battalion should conduct itself?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I did have direct contact with General Hadzihasanovic at regular and interim briefings, but my direct contact involved requesting instructions, information, et cetera: Firstly, because he was my commander and it was my duty to request such information from him; and secondly, General Hadzihasanovic had a lot of military experience, especially in terms of engaging the military police, and he had requested that I respect the norms for military police organisation and for the conduct -- for the way in which the military police should conduct themselves, and then we could discipline other members of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please have a look at document number 15. 1364 is the number of the document. This is a document that the 3rd Corps issued to all commands and independent units, and the subject is the Supreme Command Staff, a letter on respecting the law. Tell me, is this one of the documents you have mentioned, and is this -- does this show that efforts were made to respect the law -- to ensure that the law was respected in ABiH units -- or rather, the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with this document. This is one of a series of documents that defines how the law should be implemented within the units of the 3rd Corps of the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now I'll put the question to you that I asked you at the beginning, since we have had a look at all the documents now. Could you now tell me whether all these documents are examples of documents that were adopted and implemented in the 3rd Corps in relation to performing your duties -- or rather, in relation to establishing the battalion and ensuring that the law was respected in the army.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this series of documents shows some of the measures that the 3rd Corps took in order to ensure that the law was respected within the units. I'd like to emphasise the fact that, as can be seen from these documents, the 3rd Corps commander -- or rather, the 3rd Corps command attempted to inform everyone at all levels of command and control of the obligation to respect the law and to implement the prescribed norms of conduct, and in accordance with these instructions everyone at their own Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. level, in accordance with their mission and authority, had to take the necessary measures and steps to ensure that the law was respected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mujezinovic, a minute ago we had a look at a document from the Security Services Centre, from the civilian police centre, in fact. Tell me, what were the relations in the 3rd Corps, and in particular in Zenica -- what were the relations like with the civilian police? Was the military police above the civilian police? Did it have authority over the civilian police? And if not, what sort of relations were established? What were the relations like in practice?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The military police had no authority over the civilian police. The relation between -- the relationship between the civilian and military police was a relationship between partners. In order to implement the law in the territory of Zenica and elsewhere, if it was necessary, if the opportunity arose. Joint action was taken in two senses: Firstly, in specific cases when it was necessary to shed light on a crime or to detect the perpetrator of a crime. If a member of the military or a civilian was involved, then joint action would be taken. And secondly, preventive action was taken. Planned action was taken in order to implement the norms and the norms of conduct in the territory of the town of Zenica and elsewhere. This was done in order to prevent crimes from being committed and to prevent violations of public law and order, preventive action involved joint patrols, setting up joint checkpoints. And other steps were taken together for this objective.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, could you now have a look at this second section entitled "Cooperation with the civil -- with the civilian police in order to prevent criminal activities." Have a look at document under tab 20. The number of this document is 0746. Tell me, at the initial stage, does this document show that it was necessary to establish cooperation between military police units and the Zenica MUP -- or rather, the Zenica Ministry of the Interior, given the problems that existed in the town of Zenica at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This order points to that fact because at the very beginning, when the 3rd Corps was formed -- or rather, the Military Police Battalion, the main problem with regard to the work and control of members of the ABiH involved the equipment they had and the training they had because certain members firstly did not resemble soldiers, so we weren't sure whether we had any authority to check such an individual; and secondly, if such an individual didn't look like a soldier, he would just say that he was a civilian and show his identity card. And in such cases -- for this reason, this document indicates how we started cooperating with MUP, because this enabled us to take the necessary measures in the field. In the introduction, you can see that the corps commander says that there are a lot of uniformed individuals in the town and they are not members of a legal military formation, because at the time it was quite simple to obtain a full uniform and then that would provide you with protection when you wanted to commit certain crimes, especially if only the civilian police could check you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't ask you whether you were familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have a look at document under number 21 now, and tell me, given the problems encountered, do you know whether any meetings were held, whether any plans were made and adopted, or was the cooperation that you had sporadic and on a case-to-case basis?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The cooperation wasn't only on a case-to-case basis. I mentioned two aspects of cooperation: Firstly, there were situations in which we had to assist each other; and secondly - and this can be seen in this document - there was planned joint activity between the MUP, the CSB in Zenica, and the Military Police Battalion in order to take preventive measures, in order to prevent crimes from being committed or misdemeanours from being committed. And this document also states how the military police should be engaged in -- under other conditions, and this is a condition for the functioning of the civilian police too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the sake of the transcript, this is DH1601 [as interpreted]. Tell me, after these meetings -- and I can see in paragraph 2 here that your name is also mentioned. After these meetings had been held, did the chain of command change?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. There's an error in the number of the document. The document is DH160, document 1. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After these joint tasks had been established, did the chain of command change in any way in the MUP -- or rather, in the military police and the ABiH units?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't say anything about the MUP, but as far as the Military Police Battalion is concerned -- or rather, the security sector, there were no changes in command and control for the simple reason that the security service and the Military Police Battalion were equally represented. They had members from the CSB in Zenica who represented them equally. The authority for command and control was maintained, but joint activity in the field was carried out in order to implement these norms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Have a look at document 22, P299. Tell me whether you are familiar with this document and what is the subject of the document. Is the subject the same as the one that you have been testifying about so far?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm familiar with the document, and it was forwarded to units of the corps command and it deals with the subject we have mentioned, we have been talking about. The meeting was the clarify the obligations -- or rather, the competence that certain sectors had for documenting or taking disciplinary measures and the purpose was to ensure that the law was respected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have a look at document 23. 0881 is the number of this document. It's a document from the War Presidency of Zenica Municipality. And tell me, does this document speak about the need in a specific situation for the military police and civilian police to cooperate? Is this a document from the series of documents you have mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. But these conclusions weren't binding for the Military Police Battalion. It was only on the basis of agreement or orders from the corps command that the conclusions were binding or had the nature of an order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have a look at document 24, please, DH265, and the following document, since you were just talking about the necessity to respect the laws of war and the Geneva Conventions, tell me whether you also cooperated with the CSB in that field, in that area, and are you familiar with these documents and were they implemented in practice through the cooperation of the 3rd Corps military police and military -- and civilian police units.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with the documents. They're part of a series of documents that concern respecting the law and the norms of public law and order. But this attempt to guide the Security Services Centre and to implement measures which were the competence of the civilian organs -- or rather, the Ministry of the Interior, this is what the document is about. This document is about this subject.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have a look at document 25, DH161.7. Item 2 also establishes the authority that the army has -- or rather, the authority, the competence that the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior has. Are these the rules you had in mind when you were in the territory of the Zenica CSB?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from the practice established, there is the law that defines the measures that can be taken. The military police can take certain measures with regard to members of the military and the civilian police can take other measures with regard to civilians. This document supplements what I have said about civilians in uniform -- or rather, soldiers in civilian clothing who committed certain acts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have a look at the document under number 26, DH161, document 8. Is this document also about this procedure, about the way in which you cooperated in this field with the MUP organs, as stated in item 3 of the document?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The order is about cooperation, and it provides guidelines for operations in relation to crimes such as trading in weapons and ammunition. This order defines specific task, in order to prevent crime -- crimes that involved trafficking in weapons and ammunition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have a look at document 27, 1288. And before I ask you a question about this document, given everything that you have already said about establishing the battalion, et cetera, was cooperation that simple? Did it go that smoothly? Did you have problems? What sort of problems arose, if there were any problems? And how did you deal with them?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Cooperation wasn't always at the necessary level, for subjective reasons primarily. With regard to commanding the military police and the civilian police, well, no one in the command obstructed such as cooperation, but in the field - and this can be seen from the report - in certain situations civilian policemen who were used to military regime would often feel that it was their right not to get involved in joint activities. And on the basis of reports from my subordinates, I would provide the security service sector with information about these matters. And at joint meetings of the CSB and the military security and the military police, I would inform them of these problems. Naturally, there were other problems. Sometimes a military policeman wouldn't arrive on time or do what he was expected to do. So at those joint meetings, we tried to advance that cooperation and to remove any shortcomings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have a look at document 28, please, which is in the B/C/S language. There is no translation. And could you please tell us who drafted the document and could you read out the number at the top of the document so that it can later be identified, and could you tell us what the document is about. And then I will ask you a question about the document.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The document is number 04033406. That's the number. It's a record or the minutes of a meeting of a joint commission of the 3rd Corps command and the Security Services Centre in Zenica. There were three officers from the 3rd Corps - I was one of them - and from the CSB, the Security Services Centre, there were also five representatives who worked at various levels in the CSB. It's been signed by the 3rd Corps commander and the security services chief. This document advances cooperation. It's one of the joint measures taken in order to define concrete situations and measures that should be taken in concrete situations. It defines what should be undertaken and by whom in given situations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just mentioned "continued cooperation." This document is dated the 6th of September, 1993. Tell me whether the 3rd Corps command and its battalion, when implementing their policies for the security of citizens in Zenica, made such continuous efforts to cooperate with the civilian police so as to ensure that orders issued to protect civilians and their property were implemented -- or rather, to ensure that crime was prevented in that area.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: There was such continuity, which was more or less successful. That depended on the situation and the time when measures were taken. But there was continuity because neither the civilian police nor the Military Police Battalion, if they acted independently, couldn't implement all the measures prescribed by the law, especially if we go back to the subject of the equipment and training of the men of these two bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Although this is something you have spoken about a while ago - you mentioned the reasons for such cooperation - could you briefly tell us what a brigade was -- what -- why it was necessary for Military Police Battalions to have such cooperation in this area. What sort of difficulties did you encounter that resulted in you taking the measures or acting in accordance with these documents?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if there is a crime, it's necessary to go and carry out an on-site investigation to establish the factual situation and to detect the perpetrator of the crime. Then military police units, the Military Police Battalion has a problem as far as forensic equipment is concerned. How can you carry out an on-site investigation if you don't have adequate equipment. The CSB for a long time after 1993 had the men and the equipment to take fingerprints at the scene of a crime, to carry out a ballistic analysis for certain situations, to take the paraffin glove test to determine whether firearms had been used. That's one aspect of cooperation. And then secondly, if you come across someone disturbing law and order by opening fire from arms, he might show you his identity card and say he's a civilian. If you don't have a joint patrol that can check this person's identity immediately, you won't be able to take any measures. And if only the police appears and he says that he's a member of the army, then this individual can continue to do what he was doing. This is the reverse situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Given all the authority you had, measures you could take to prevent members of the army from committing crimes or to prevent them from disobeying orders, tell me, in what way could army members be held to account?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they could be held accountable in the following way: Disciplinary measures could be taken within the units that they were members of; misdemeanour proceedings could be instituted against them for having violated public law and order; and naturally, criminal proceedings could be instituted against them for having committed an offence of that kind. It depended on the crime, on the act committed, which body would be responsible for the crime and responsible for filing a report. The civilian police would be responsible for civilians and they'd file reports with misdemeanour courts. But other measures were taken at all levels of command and control. This depended on the seriousness of the crime. And measures were taken in accordance with the Law on Criminal Procedure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, how important in preventing crime was the issuance of concrete and specific orders as to how members of the army should act?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The orders were the guiding factor which facilitated the work of the military police in enforcing preventing -- preventing measures against all forms of crime and disciplinary offences. Why? Because the unit commanders within the 3rd Corps were informed and held responsible for taking preventive measures. They had to prevent such acts at their level. So as a result, the work of the military police is 50 per cent Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. facilitated, and then through patrol services and other ways we tried to act preventively but the orders clearly defined the tasks and competencies, so it is not necessary to explain it each time to everyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the previous documents we've looked at, we can see that there is reference to the escalation of criminal activity, looting, et cetera. As there was a war on, did the 3rd Corps through its acts and orders clearly define war booty, and was this of significance for your activities in preventing and discovering perpetrators of criminal offences during times of war?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: From the General Staff through the corps commands, we received certain documents defining "war booty." From the level of the 3rd Corps command and in accordance with those orders and reports from the ground, certain instructions and orders were issued defining the procedure when it comes to war booty. Full respect of those orders should have led to a fully regulating -- regulated system and respect of norms with regard to war booty. These orders facilitated the work of the military police on the ground because consistent implementation of the order would not require any engagement by the military police but all orders were not always fully implemented and that is when the military police and other command entities were obliged to prevent or request full respect of the instructions on war booty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the break, you probably looked at document at tab 29, number 1695, "Procedure with war booty," then the document at tab 30, DH161/3, the document at tab 31, 0887, and document at tab 32, number 0917, and document at tab 33, 1469. And my first question is: When you look at these documents, can you tell me whether you were aware of these documents and their contents?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was familiar with documents of this kind, and they actually reflect what I just said. You have this document, 1469, of the chief of the security sector forwarding Supreme Command instructions, and in accordance with the situation on the ground, they defined the procedure with respect to war booty, the aim being to pre-empt any criminal activity and abuse of a position on -- of various kinds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your testimony so far, you spoke about your tasks in disciplining the army and the fact that clear orders indicated how you and the subordinate units had to behave and what measures should be taken, as well as how to establish whether those orders were being fully abided by. Will you now tell me: When it comes to the obligation to file criminal reports for criminal offences, was the 3rd Corps satisfied by simply issuing the order that every perpetrator had to be criminally prosecuted or was there also the obligation to inform those issuing such orders of their implementation?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: In principle, all orders of the corps command had a paragraph defining reporting and a proposal of measures to fully implement that order. The same applied to this order on sanctioning and filing of criminal reports for criminal offences. The Military Police Battalion and other units from the 3rd Corps were obliged to submit reports or an analysis of various groups of criminal offences. As far as I know, the corps command was not satisfied with these reports alone but would occasionally organise meetings with the people responsible from district military courts and prosecutor's offices and the immediate commanding officers on the ground so as to channel the work in the field and the proper filing of criminal reports. There is no point in filing an incorrect report, so the corps command, in addition to orders, went a step further and organised joint meetings with that aim in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you look at document 34, DH168, and just tell me whether you are aware that in this way the command asked for information from subordinate units about filing of criminal reports.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Among others, the unit I was in command of had the obligation to submit such reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In connection with discipline in the army, you have spoken at some length. Now will you please look at a number of documents and tell me whether these were orders binding for the military police and were these orders conducive to crime prevention and the disciplining of the army. The first such document that we can look at before the break is at tab 35. It is numbered DH161. Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And it is addressed to all subordinate units, and it has to do with the soldier-like appearance of members of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To what extent did you have ongoing or occasional problems with the implementation of this order or failure to respect it?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Problems were of a lasting nature, but the intensity varied, depending on the situation. Justification for failure to observe this order was often found in the fact that people were away a lot and questions linked to mobilisation. But what assisted us in particular, that the insignia of the BH army would immediately eliminate civilians who were wearing uniforms without the insignia, so it was easier for us to identify members of the 3rd Corps as a result.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this justification tolerated, or did the military police take measures if they come across a soldier behaving contrary to this order?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The military police, implementing its powers, would first caution the person, and if the person was not wearing the proper insignia, he would be handed over to his own unit with a request that appropriate measures be taken. In drastic cases, measures envisaged by the law were taken. But this was mostly dealt with at the level of disciplinary measures or punishment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps this would be the best time for the break, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I note that we will have three-quarters of an hour left, and there are still dozens of documents left. What do you intend to do?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I abided by the suggestion to show each document to the witness, and this takes time. And I suggest, since this second batch of documents mainly deals with orders to discipline the army and that these are documents for which English translations exist and 90 per cent of those documents are already in evidence, that I be allowed after the witness has looked through these documents that I ask him only a few questions about these documents, without having to go from one to the other again, because clearly these are documents which we have tendered into evidence through other witnesses. These were documents that were already identified and commented on by previous witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Again, that's the point. The documents are in already, and other witnesses have testified about that, so I object to any leading form of inviting the witness to make a -- sort of a kitchen-sink comment about what the 3rd Corps has done. He can do it as long as it comes within his purview of the commander of the police battalion. That's fine. But just these leading questions at the end of examination: Do all these documents show, blah, blah, blah, and then he only can say yes, I object to that form of questioning. But if the documents are in, that's fine for -- for closing arguments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I suppose that the Defence will not ask leading questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am endeavouring not to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Major, during the break, look through the remaining documents, and we will try and finish with the examination-in-chief, at least, today, because I assume that the Prosecution will want to have the same amount of time, which will take us through tomorrow, and I don't know whether we'll even have time for the re-examination and the questions of Judges. It is 25 to 1.00, and we will resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. We're waiting for the accused. We can resume now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mujezinovic, you spoke about numerous measures and steps that you undertook in the orders you implemented. Would you please look at document at tab 39, and tell me, do you recognise this document and what does it represent? It is DH155, document number 3.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I do know the document, and it is a report on the engagement of the Military Police Battalion, sent to the chief of security of the 3rd Corps. It's a regular monthly report on elements provided by the security sector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The data contained in this report, whose activities do they refer to? Are they the activities of the battalion or of the military police as a whole?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: These are reports on the engagement of the Military Police Battalion and the elements that are referred to, but a report of a similar content compiles the data received from military police companies in the brigades.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document refers to certain assignments that you carried out. You said that a part of the battalion sometimes took part in combat activities. The numbers in paragraph 2, "Participation in combat activities," does it show that parts of the battalion in view of the situation were sometimes directly engaged in combat as soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, members of the Military Police Battalion, like all other members of the ABiH, had the duty and right to take part in combat activities when so requested by the superior commander. We see that 22 military policemen were directly engaged in combat at Putis locality and 32 military policemen at Zepce locality. Some were directly engaged and others indirectly to control the territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said earlier that orders were guidelines for your own activities. Look at this, application of military police measures against members of the army, and under A, it says that "The identity of 22.700 members of the army were -- was checked," and in B, it says how many people were detained. Is this report a typical example of the range of activities engaged in by the Military Police Battalion or does this reflect an exceptional situation when you had so much work to do in one month?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: No, this reflects the normal engagement of the battalion in that period. What I can point out is that if we look at it more closely, regarding the number of 22.700 members of the army being identified, it has to do with regular vehicle road checks and also patrol work and operative work and in carrying out security activities. Some IDs were checked during action around corps commands. Anyone coming to the command, his identity had to be checked when visiting. As for the 256 individuals who were detained, these numbers provide a cross-section of the activities over a period of one month.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 2, Chapter 4, "Criminal and disciplinary reports," under A it says what -- for what criminal acts criminal reports were filed during that month. And on page 4, under C, it says that "About 350 interviews were conducted and on record statements were taken from about 120 individuals." Is this the work done by the small group of your inspectors consisting of eight to ten men, as you said, in the services department?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This small group of the Military Police Battalion, after interviewing people, they had to take on record statements, and here reference is made to 120 individuals. And after this interview, people were asked to give statements and -- or not to give statements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, Mr. Mujezinovic, the procedure, from the moment you became aware that a criminal act had been committed to the filing of a criminal report, was the procedure always the same? Was it always possible to find the perpetrator, or were different procedures and methods applied until the stage of filing criminal reports?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: There were different procedures applied by the Military Police Battalion. The best solution for discovering the perpetrators of criminal offences is -- the military police is on the spot when an act is being committed, to prevent it or to arrest the perpetrator. But the most frequent situation was that the military police would come to the scene after the act had been committed. After securing the scene and collecting evidence, a plan is drafted implying collecting operative information in the aim of discovering the perpetrators of the act. I will go back to the question of equipment and resources. The military police didn't have highly sophisticated methods to detect and discover perpetrators. Why? Because we lacked the appropriate means. For instance, fingerprints. Even if we were able to take fingerprints, we didn't have a database with all fingerprints recorded. This applied to other methods too. The main method applied was to interview eyewitnesses, potential eyewitnesses, or co-perpetrators, and this meant that it took some time to collect all the evidence. And after collecting sufficient substantive evidence, we would prepare a report to the competent prosecutor's office and only then would we arrest the person who committed the act.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, were there cases when you had to spend several months before you discovered perpetrators? And were you sometimes involved in such procedures?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. There were all the aggravating factors in the functioning of the army as a whole, and these were constraints on the battalion as well. More specifically, due to the poor flow of information because of difficulties in information exchange, because of the impossibility to reach the scene in time, it would happen that it would take us some time to collect operative information and all the other elements required for a criminal report. Frequently there were several criminal acts that took place at the same time. For example, the example of the Green Legion, a formation that was part of the 3rd Corps and whose members were particularly prominent in criminal activities. But it took us time for us to collect the documents and the material evidence, and of course with the security sector we submitted all this to the prosecutor's office, and when they accepted it as relevant on the basis of a plan did we actually arrest and escort people to the court. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you now look at document at tab 79 and read out who issued the document and what it is about, as it is a document in B/C/S only. Tell me, is this document related to what you have just been telling us in any way?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the document that relates to the plan of activities to arrest members of the Green Legion, the code name was Golub, or "pigeon," and it is the climax of the operative work from the moment the act was committed to the arrest of the suspects.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document is dated the 12th of January, 1994. It has the ERN number 04034202. Please look at page 3 of this document. What does it represent, ERN 04034204?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Command of the action. This is actually the team that will coordinate and be in charge of this operation. As these were members of the 314th Brigade, then the assistant commander for security of that brigade took part in the preparations for the criminal report. As I was the commander of the unit that was supposed to arrest the persons listed and Mr. Ramiz Dugalic, chief of security, as the superior to me and to Mr. Balavac, and also as the person responsible for coordinating all these activities, constituted this team.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, was part of your responsibility to secure the reception centre for prisoners of war, the centre for the reception of prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This centre was formed as early as 1992, and it was within the jurisdiction of the district police or the District Staff of Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. With the formation of the 3rd Corps, this jurisdiction was transferred and the centre became part of the KP Dom of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the 3rd Corps, was there any policy with respect to how and when prisoners of war captured in combat should be transferred to the reception centre in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: There was an established procedure in the 3rd Corps when it comes to the treatment of prisoners of war. According to information available to me, the procedure was as follows: The unit that actually captures an enemy soldier -- or rather, the security organ and the intelligence organ of that unit carries out the initial interrogation to collect potentially needed information about the deployment of the enemy and his weapons, and then together with a report to the chief of the security sector, the persons are escorted to the centre for the reception of prisoners of war. If the chief of security on the basis of this report assesses that this is a large group of prisoners of war or prisoners of special importance, or if he should decide on his own, he may engage a Military Police Battalion to escort prisoners of war to the centre for the reception of prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since part of the Military Police Battalion from the 3rd Corps provided security for the reception centre for prisoners of war, did you in the battalion ever receive any information on prisoners being maltreated in the place where they had previously been detained until they were taken to the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I personally didn't speak to the prisoners of war or to any other suspects, but on the basis of the reports from subordinates, I didn't receive any information according to which there were such situations in other places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever receive an official criminal report on the mistreatment of POWs taken to the KP Dom who had previously been held in some unit's detention unit, in the unit -- in a detention unit of a unit that had captured him?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't receive any official report, a document of any kind about such matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, tell me whether in this reception centre, which was part of the 3rd Corps and part of your battalion provided security for it -- in this reception centre, was it possible for the International Red Cross to gain access? Was it possible for other international representatives to gain access to this centre in order to control, to check the situation in which prisoners of war were kept there?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The reception centre for prisoners of war made it possible for others to gain access if the rules were followed. This involved announcing the visit to the 3rd Corps command and documents granting authority to visit the centre should be issued. There were no time limits. It was possible to visit the centre at any time if the relevant organ had issued authorisation. Visits were then made, as far as I know, almost on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As the battalion commander, did you ever receive information of any kind, a complaint, according to which battalion members or someone else had mistreated prisoners of war in the reception centre?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: On the contrary, I heard a lot of praise, especially from members of the International Red Cross. They said that the centre for POWs was professional and the conditions were the best-possible conditions for the detainees there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We heard about the battalion engaging in combat action a while ago. Tell me whether in the course of its police duties -- was the battalion ever involved in certain actions that ensued after combat action in a given area?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were various situations in which the Military Police Battalion was engaged. I remember that as early as the beginning of 1993 - I think it was towards the end of January - we received our first concrete task. The battalion was to take a large group of POWs from the Dusina area to some other area. I received this order from the chief of the security sector, and I think that in the late afternoon or in the evening a group of about 20 prisoners were taken away after the conflict in Dusina. They were taken away. They were taken away in -- in a bus. The military police provided security. And they were placed in the Centre for Receiving Prisoners of War that very same issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any tasks or did you issue any tasks with your members with regard to the events in Dusina in addition to the task you had to take over and transfer prisoners to the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: That evening I immediately informed the chief of the security sector and on the following day I had two duties to perform: Firstly - I think it was in the morning - the duty officer from the duty centre through his commander informed me that he had received information from the civilian protection, or from the morgue - I'm not sure - according to which a certain number of corpses had been delivered. I think there were about ten even. They'd been delivered to the cantonal hospital morgue. In accordance with the rules for the military police, the duty officer informed the duty investigating judge at the military court. A team was formed and sent to the site to carry out an on-site investigation. At the same time, I informed the chief of security of these matters, and he said that since the judge was at the scene, I should follow the instructions and start interviewing people who had arrived in the Centre for POWs. When this team returned from the site, I was informed by the commander of military police investigations that the on-site investigation -- the Security Services Centre had carried out the concrete investigation, because we weren't capable of doing so, but the investigative judge ordered that we should take statements from individuals who had been taken to the Centre for POWs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this done? Were you informed about this -- or rather, do you know what the results were of the interviews conducted?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the general results of the interviews. I didn't try to analyse them. All I know for sure is that the commander, the person in command of the military police investigations, informed me that there was nothing in particular to be pointed out with regard to the prisoners of war, that all the documents were in accordance with the law -- all the documents in accordance with the law and the rules for the military police had been provided to the investigative judge. A copy was provided to him that had been signed, and one copy of all the statements were forwarded to the chief of the security services. Afterwards, as far as I know, we didn't have any additional tasks. We didn't have to carry out any other investigations, as far as the POWs are concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With regard to the situation that the investigative judge was in, who went to the scene of the crime, who could provide you -- who could issue you other tasks to check new information, new facts?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: This was the responsibility of the judge in charge of the on-site investigation -- or rather, in charge of the entire case. He was the person who was responsible and who was in control of all these elements. He would make his own assessments and then issue instructions to us or to someone else in the Security Services Centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, in addition to the case, when you were involved in certain police activities after combat, did you as the battalion -- or rather, the battalion commander issue any other orders for any other measures to be taken in relation to other combat ongoing in the territory of the 3rd Corps? Were there any other cases in which the military police was engaged?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember any other particular engagement during that period. I think that in the second half we had some police duties in the area of Kakanj or Zepce. It depended on the intensity of the fighting in the field. But I don't think that we had any other activities later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did some of the military police go to Guca Gora in accordance with the order that we saw a minute ago? And if so, what sort of task did you assign to that part of the battalion?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: You're referring to Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: In accordance with an order from the corps command, a mixed patrol -- a platoon was formed and sent to the field. Its main task was to report to the command of the 306th and to act in accordance with the assessment of the 306th command. They had to take the measures that they were told to take.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Kakanj a minute ago. In the area of Kakanj, was there a feature of a similar kind, similar to Guca Gora, and did the battalion have any tasks in relation to that feature?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: In Kakanj? In the territory of Kakanj, similar action was taken in the direction of Kraljeva Sutjeska, again with a unit of the military police from the 309th which had territorial jurisdiction. The main task was to prevent any crimes and to take preventive action when crimes were -- had already been committed, they had to record them and file reports to the court -- with the court and take measures in accordance with the instructions issued by the judge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just tell us why Kraljeva Sutjeska is important.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: There is a monastery there as well, I think, since that area was inhabited mostly by Croats and after the fighting -- on the first day after disarmament, there was looting, buildings were set on fire, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether you have any information about whether that monastery in Kraljeva Sutjeska was efficiently protected from damage of any kind being inflicted on it, as was the case for the Guca Gora monastery.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: According to the information I had, it was protected to the extent that this was possible. According to my information, the commander of a unit was even replaced there for failing to take preventive action and to take the necessary measures in time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, what sort of tasks -- or rather, first of all, did the battalion have any tasks with relation to providing security and ensuring that UNHCR convoys could pass through in safety, as well as other representatives of international organisations? And did you engage members of the Military Police Battalion for such tasks?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: One of our tasks, among other things, was to provide security for various international organisations passing through the territory, and some units from the military police were engaged if this was necessary in the opinion of the chief of security, and he would suggest to the 3rd Corps commander that the military police be engaged in such cases. I think there were such situations, but this was most evident in the Ticici area when a military battalion provided as part of its mission security and also escorted a UNHCR convoy, probably because of the difficult situation, because of hunger, et cetera, a large group of citizens intercepted the convoy. There were some uniformed individuals within this group. After the convoy had been intercepted and after a short discussion, an armed attack was carried out on the military police patrol. Although we sustained losses - three or four soldiers were wounded; one of them was seriously wounded. Topalovic, I think, who was subsequently declared to be a 70 per cent invalid - in spite of this, we managed to secure the majority of the convoy and continue. At the time, since there weren't many policemen, we couldn't do anything else. And after the convoy arrived at its destination, after having carried out an on-site investigation, we formed a joint team with a patrol -- or rather, with the Kakanj police station. We found out -- we obtained certain information, and as far as I know, criminal reports were filed with the prosecutor's office against a number of individuals, members of the military and civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, was the Military Police Battalion engaged in some way to find the kidnappers of Zivko Totic?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As soon as we heard about the incident with Mr. Totic, the chief of the security service ordered me to act together with the judge from the military court and with an HVO team, a team of HVO police and civilian police. I was ordered to go to the site, to carry out an on-site investigation. Through the commander, I sent a team to the site. They were at the on-site investigation, but there was tension between the HVO, the police, and the army at the time because the initial information that they provided was that this was what the army had done -- or rather, the military police. And afterwards, in accordance with instructions from the security sector, I was ordered to separate a team that would be at the disposal of a mixed team formed of army members and the police and other structures, and the HVO probably. The objective was to go to any places that the kidnappers might be using and to check these places. It depended on the situation, but I would engage a detachment or a platoon - it depended on the area we went to and what we were looking for. But at the same time, the chief of security ordered me to use some of the men who Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. weren't engaged in the field and to use them for -- to gather operative information on those who may have committed the crime or to obtain information on where these individuals might be staying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, after that initial stage, after these activities were halted and since some Mujahedin appeared as the kidnappers, tell me whether the corps commander ever assigned you a task in relation to this event, and if so, what sort of task were you assigned?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I was assigned a task and later I found out that it was directly related to this affair. The commander ordered me to have a unit at the level of a company to be ready to intervene. On his orders, I then found out that this company was to be in a state of readiness in case it was necessary to provide protection or to carry out certain other activities when Mr. Totic was being exchanged in the Hotel Internacional, through the intermediary of some international organisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was this company that you had in a state of readiness, the company that was to be engaged upon the commander's order, and how soon -- how fast could it go into action if it was necessary for it to do so?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The company was in the Zenica KP Dom -- or rather, in the barracks of the military police. The barracks is about a kilometre from Hotel Internacional -- between a kilometre and a half and two kilometres. I assume that the commander had the option of engaging the military police because when there's not much traffic, the military police can be at the site very quickly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fortunately, that company wasn't engaged.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: No. And as I said, subsequently I found out that it was in a state of readiness for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, have a look at document under number 70 now -- in this document number 80, DH155/2 [realtime transcript read in error "DH152/2"]. Tell me, do you know what sort of document this is?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: This is a report on criminal reports filed and on what was requested of us in the security sector. It concerns the date the 14th of September, 1992 to the 1st of March, 1994. I don't know why the security sector wanted a full analysis, but it was my duty to provide such analysis. And this report was drafted on the basis of what my associates prepared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under C on page 1, you can see the structure of reported persons, and we can see that 17 officers from the ABiH were reported. Tell me, when criminal reports were filed, were they filed in the same way for officers of the ABiH as for other army members when crimes were committed?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, naturally. Any members of the ABiH, regardless of their ranks and status, were equally responsible in the eyes of the law. The Military Police Battalion tried to abide by the law to the extent that this was possible in such a situation, and they tried to do this regardless of the status of the perpetrator of a crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under the structure of crimes, in paragraph 6 it says that for the crime of falsely identifying oneself, two criminal reports were filed during this period of time. What I'm interested in is: How common was this crime of falsely identifying oneself and are those the only reports that were filed for such acts?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: The crime of falsely identifying oneself or false impersonation provided individuals with certain benefits, and one could record such cases when criminal reports were filed. Here there are two criminal reports, but we can't see against how many individuals. That's the first thing. It could have concerned more than two individuals. And secondly, this crime was usually committed in conjunction with a more serious crime, which was punishable, because usually false impersonation usually resulted in burglary or even murder. So false impersonation was usually treated -- well, in these two cases, it was treated in this way because false impersonation results in more serious crimes and we would take this into consideration when punishing a perpetrator of such a crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If a civilian identified himself as a member of the military, who would file reports and which organs would then deal with false impersonation?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: If false impersonation doesn't result in appropriating military property, then it's the civilian police's responsibility to file criminal reports -- or rather, the civilian is held accountable for a civilian court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll take advantage of the opportunity -- I'll take advantage of the fact that during the break you had a look at this entire series of documents from number -- from document number 58, document 0972, DH278, 1127, DH283, 1289, 1290, DH1311, then 1432, 1452, 1453, 1456, 1471, 1477, 1478, 1481, 1488, 1517, 1548, 1553, DH1560 ID, DH286, and under number 80, DH155/2. Tell me, within these documents, do you recognise criminal reports filed by your battalion -- or rather prosecutor's requests made on the basis of criminal reports from the Military Police Battalion? And you have provided us with -- or you provided summary information in the report that we were just commenting on.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: In the documents that you have just listed, it's easy to recognise the criminal reports filed by the Military Police Battalion. I'd like to emphasise the fact that criminal reports contain elements in accordance with the instructions that we received from the prosecutor's office, but this wasn't restrictive in the sense of determining responsibility or describing the crime for which an individual should be held responsible. After the criminal report had been provided, the investigative judge would take a decision -- or rather, the military prosecutor would bring an indictment against a certain individual, and then there would be a decision on carrying out an investigation and certain tasks -- concrete tasks would be issued in that document with regard to taking certain measures. For example, with regard to the Military Police Battalion, it would -- they would state whether it was necessary to gather more evidence, take statements, and then there would be the criminal proceedings that would be instituted in accordance with the law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Mujezinovic, when you now look back at the year 1993 during which you were the Military Police Battalion commander and you took measures to establish it, to make sure that it could carry out all of the tasks that you had to carry out -- tell me, when you now look back to that period of time, did you do everything that could be done under those conditions to prevent crimes from being committed and to find and process the perpetrators of such crimes?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC
utterances.text: I think so -- well, I don't think so. I'm quite sure that I did so, since I had superiors who wouldn't allow me to think about anything else other than processing individuals and taking measures in accordance with the law. When I say that I'm certain about this, if we take into -- into consideration the conditions under which the police -- the military police and the ABiH lived, then I'm quite sure that given the men I had and the equipment I had, given all the difficulties, all the problems that hadn't been resolved, as far as the organisation of the state and system were concerned, given all these problems that we had, from feeding soldiers -- including feeding soldiers and other things, then I believe that the Military Police Battalion overcame these difficulties to the extent it was possible and respected the chain of command, respected the law, respected the rules for the conduct of the military police, and took the necessary measures to act preventively -- or rather, to find perpetrators of the crimes, to gather evidence, to file criminal reports and reports to the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mujezinovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this concludes my examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll continue tomorrow. General Kubura's Defence, do they intend to ask any questions? And if so, how long will they take?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we will have a few questions for this witness, but it will not take more than 15 to 20 minutes. And I think that our learned colleagues said that they would not use the whole day for the cross-examination, so we will be able to fit it in tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution, how long do you plan to take for the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Well, before the break I thought I could finish, but unfortunately Dusina was mentioned again, and it wasn't contained in the 65 ter summary, so I certainly will use the afternoon to -- to see how we can deal with that, and I'll do my best to finish within -- you know, before the second break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If necessary, we always have Thursday at our disposal. Major, you will come back for the hearing beginning at 9.00 tomorrow. In the meantime, you will not meet with the parties. As you have taken the solemn declaration, you are now a witness of justice, so you are prohibited from contacting anyone. And you will be back here at 9.00 tomorrow. We have extended our hearing by five minutes, and I apologise mainly to the interpreters. I invite you all to be back here tomorrow at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 16th day of March, 2005, at 9.00 a.m. 25
